components.note: 匕 (a kneeling person) — a mourner bowed down in grief.
歹 (skeletal remains) — the corpse being mourned, the source of 死's meaning 'to die, dead.'

example.hanzi: 警方还没有公布死者的身份。
example.pinyin: Jǐngfāng hái méiyǒu gōngbù sǐzhě de shēnfèn.
example.english: The police have not yet released the identity of the deceased.
example.fact: 死者 is built transparently from 死 ("to die") plus 者, a nominalizing suffix meaning "the one who/that," the same suffix behind 读者 ("reader") and 作者 ("author") — but its formal, news-register tone means everyday speech more often just names the person directly rather than reaching for this somewhat clinical term.

components.note: 亻 (person) — 傻 describes a state of mind a person is in.
囟 (the top of the head), together with a striking motion below, pictures someone being hit on the head — the odd image behind 傻's meaning 'foolish.'
Represents the round shape of a melon hanging on the vine.

example.hanzi: 你怎么会相信这种谎话?真是个傻瓜。
example.pinyin: Nǐ zěnme huì xiāngxìn zhè zhǒng huǎnghuà? Zhēn shi ge shǎguā.
example.english: How could you believe such a lie? What a fool.
example.fact: 瓜 (melon) shows up in more than one Mandarin word for foolishness — 傻瓜 ("foolish melon") sits alongside Sichuanese slang like 瓜娃子 ("silly kid") — a folk association between a round, hollow melon and an empty head that spans both standard Mandarin and regional dialect.

meanings: mile (unit of length equal to 1.609 km)

components.note: 艹 (plant) — 英 originally meant 'flower, blossom,' later borrowed for 'outstanding, hero' and to write 'England, English.'
央 (yāng) gives a sound hint — 英 is pronounced yīng, sharing the initial consonant and a nasal final, though the vowel has shifted.
田 (farmland) over 土 (earth/soil) — originally referred to a village or a measured unit of farmland, later extended to mean 'inside' or a unit of distance.

example.hanzi: 从这里到机场大约十五英里。
example.pinyin: Cóng zhèlǐ dào jīchǎng dàyuē shíwǔ yīnglǐ.
example.english: It's about fifteen miles from here to the airport.
example.fact: 英里 literally means "English li" — 英 is the character used to transliterate "England/English" (as in 英国, 英语), attached to 里 (a traditional Chinese distance unit) to name the foreign, imperial-system mile. Mainland China's everyday distance unit is instead the metric 公里 ("common/metric li," kilometer), so 英里 mostly turns up when discussing English-speaking countries.

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 挑 describes an action done with the hand, picking or carrying.
兆 (zhào) gives a sound distantly related to tiāo, having drifted apart over time.
戈 (a dagger-axe, a weapon) — 战 relates to fighting and war.
占 (zhàn) gives the sound — 战 is also pronounced zhàn, an exact match.

example.hanzi: 这个项目对我们团队是一个很大的挑战。
example.pinyin: Zhège xiàngmù duì wǒmen tuánduì shì yí gè hěn dà de tiǎozhàn.
example.english: This project is a huge challenge for our team.
example.fact: 挑战 does double duty as both a verb ("to challenge someone," 挑战权威 "challenge authority") and a noun ("a challenge," as here) without changing form — a common pattern in Chinese verb-object compounds, where English usually needs two different words (challenge vs. challenging) to cover the same ground.

components.note: 匕 (a kneeling person) — a mourner bowed down in grief.
歹 (skeletal remains) — the corpse being mourned, the source of 死's meaning 'to die, dead.'

example.hanzi: 他的祖父几年前已经死去了。
example.pinyin: Tā de zǔfù jǐ nián qián yǐjīng sǐqù le.
example.english: His grandfather died several years ago.
example.fact: 去 here works as a directional verb complement rather than "to go" — attached after 死, it marks the action as a complete departure from life, the same abstract "away, off" sense 去 contributes in 失去 ("to lose," lit. "lose away") and 除去 ("to remove").

components.note: A short stroke placed above a longer one — a simple graphic way to show 'up' or 'above,' contrasted with 下 (down), which flips the strokes.

example.hanzi: 电梯坏了,我们只能走上去。
example.pinyin: Diàntī huài le, wǒmen zhǐ néng zǒu shàngqù.
example.english: The elevator is broken, so we can only walk up.
example.fact: 上去 and its mirror image 上来 both mean "to go/come up," but the choice of 去 versus 来 encodes the speaker's own viewpoint — 上去 moves away from the speaker's position, 上来 moves toward it, a directional distinction with no separate word in English.

components.note: 耳 (ear) — an old link between listening to official duties and 职's meaning 'duty, profession, office'
只 (zhī) gives a loose sound connection to 职's reading zhí

example.hanzi: 你的职业是什么?
example.pinyin: Nǐ de zhíyè shì shénme?
example.english: What is your profession?
example.fact: 职业 leans formal and written — the word you'd fill in on a form or see printed on an ID card — while everyday spoken Mandarin more often just asks 你是做什么工作的? ("What kind of work do you do?"), a case where a concept's dictionary word isn't quite the most natural thing to say out loud.

components.note: 土 (earth/soil) — 地's original meaning is 'earth, ground'
也 (yě) gives a partial sound match for 地's other reading dì; in this grammatical-particle usage the character is instead pronounced 'de'
Earth — a site is a piece of land.
Gives the sound zhǐ, matching the character's reading.

example.hanzi: 请把你的地址写在这张纸上。
example.pinyin: Qǐng bǎ nǐ de dìzhǐ xiě zài zhè zhāng zhǐ shàng.
example.english: Please write your address on this piece of paper.
example.fact: 地址 has extended naturally into the digital world as 网址 ("web address," lit. "net-address") and IP 地址 ("IP address") — the same 址 root, originally just "the location of a place" (built from 土 earth + 止 a footprint/stopping-place), now covers both physical mail and internet locations.

components.note: The oracle-bone form has been interpreted as a bird flying up toward the sky; the meaning later shifted entirely to represent negation, 'not.'
少 depicts a few small dots or grains, like scattered sand — a simple picture of a small quantity, giving the meaning 'few' or 'little.'

example.hanzi: 这次比赛来了不少观众。
example.pinyin: Zhè cì bǐsài lái le bùshǎo guānzhòng.
example.english: Quite a few spectators came to this match.
example.fact: 不少 is a double negative that reads as a plain positive — literally "not few," it lands as "quite a lot," similar to how English "not a little" can imply a fair amount — except in Chinese 不少 is the completely neutral, everyday way to say this, not a marked or literary construction.

components.note: 土 (earth/soil) — 地's original meaning is 'earth, ground'
也 (yě) gives a partial sound match for 地's other reading dì; in this grammatical-particle usage the character is instead pronounced 'de'
犭 (dog) on the left represents a guard dog.
讠 (speech) suggests an accusation or a legal case being spoken.
犬 (dog) on the right completes the scene, giving 狱 its meaning 'prison, lawsuit.'

example.hanzi: 那部电影把战场描述得像地狱一样。
example.pinyin: Nà bù diànyǐng bǎ zhànchǎng miáoshù de xiàng dìyù yíyàng.
example.english: That movie described the battlefield as being like hell.
example.fact: 地狱 ("earth-prison") entered Chinese primarily as a Buddhist translation term for the underworld realm of punishment (Naraka) — distinct from 阴间, the older native folk term for the land of the dead, a reminder that Buddhism's arrival in China left its mark even on ordinary vocabulary for the afterlife.

components.note: Traditionally analyzed as 日 combined with 疋, linked to the idea of speaking directly and truthfully — the source of 是's meaning 'to be, indeed, right.'

example.hanzi: 天开始下雨了,于是我们决定回家。
example.pinyin: Tiān kāishǐ xiàyǔ le, yúshì wǒmen juédìng huí jiā.
example.english: It started raining, so we decided to go home.
example.fact: 于是 links two clauses in a strict cause-then-effect sequence and always follows the cause — unlike 因为...所以... it can't front the reason first — making it closer to English "and so" or "thereupon," narrating what happened next rather than formally explaining why.

components.note: A picture of a nose; because people in ancient China would point to their own nose when referring to themselves, the character came to mean 'self.'
Originally depicted a hand 扌 gripping a weapon 戈; this original meaning was later borrowed to represent the pronoun 'I/we.'

example.hanzi: 每个人都应该学会自我反省。
example.pinyin: Měi gè rén dōu yīnggāi xuéhuì zìwǒ fǎnxǐng.
example.english: Everyone should learn to reflect on themselves.
example.fact: 自我 almost always attaches as a prefix before another verb or noun — 自我反省 ("self-reflection"), 自我介绍 ("self-introduction"), 自我保护 ("self-protection") — rather than standing alone the way English "self" can; for a stand-alone reflexive pronoun, Chinese instead reaches for 自己.

meanings: (dialect) (usu. used in the negative) to get along with (sb)

components.note: 又 (hand) and 寸 (also derived from a hand shape) — together suggesting two hands matching or corresponding, related to 对's meaning 'correct, matching.'
亻 (a person) — someone receiving something
寸 (a hand) — a hand handing something over

example.hanzi: 这种情况我们该怎么对付?
example.pinyin: Zhè zhǒng qíngkuàng wǒmen gāi zěnme duìfu?
example.english: How should we deal with this kind of situation?
example.fact: 对付 usually carries a faint sense of makeshift or reluctant effort — "handling" something you'd rather not have to — which is why it also extends to 对付一下 ("make do for now") in a way that the more neutral, businesslike 处理 ("to handle, process") does not.

meanings: good action, deed, thing or work
Daoist or Buddhist ceremony for the souls of the dead

components.note: 女 (woman) — represents a mother.
子 (child/son) — a mother together with her child was seen as an image of goodness, giving 好 its meaning 'good.'

example.hanzi: 帮助别人是一件好事。
example.pinyin: Bāngzhù biérén shì yí jiàn hǎoshì.
example.english: Helping others is a good thing.
example.fact: 好事 is a case where tone alone splits two unrelated words: read hǎoshì (as here) it means "a good deed"; read hàoshì — identical characters, different tones — it instead becomes an adjective for someone "meddlesome, eager to stir up trouble." Context and tone, not spelling, are all that separate a compliment from a complaint.

components.note: 礻 (spirit, ritual) — 祈 concerns communicating with the spirits or gods.
斤 (jīn) gives a sound distantly related to qí, having drifted apart over time.
礻 (spirit) — 祷 concerns communicating with the spirits or gods.
寿 (shòu) gives a sound distantly related to dǎo, having drifted apart over time.

example.hanzi: 她闭上眼睛,轻声祈祷。
example.pinyin: Tā bìshàng yǎnjīng, qīngshēng qídǎo.
example.english: She closed her eyes and prayed quietly.
example.fact: Both halves of 祈祷 carry the 礻 radical — a simplified altar/spirit-tablet shape also seen in 神 ("god") and 祝 ("to wish, bless") — marking the word as belonging to a whole family of characters tied to ritual and worship.

components.note: 攵 (a hand with an implement) — relates to 收's meaning 'to receive, collect, harvest.'
丩 (jiū) served as the phonetic base; its pronunciation has since drifted well away from shōu.
扌 (hand) — picking something up is done with the hand.
合 (to gather, combine) contributes to the character's form, describing the action of gathering things up.

example.hanzi: 出门前,请把房间收拾好。
example.pinyin: Chūmén qián, qǐng bǎ fángjiān shōushi hǎo.
example.english: Before going out, please tidy up the room.
example.fact: 收拾 can shift from its literal "tidy up, pack" sense into a colloquial threat — 我要收拾你了 means "I'm going to sort you out" — using the verb the same way English "sort out" can describe either organizing a room or handling a person roughly.

components.note: 宀 (roof) — represents a home.
各 (each, various) — a person arriving from elsewhere and welcomed under one's roof gave 客 its meaning 'guest, visitor.'
A simple line drawing of a person's legs seen from the side, used to depict a human being.

example.hanzi: 今晚家里有客人,我们得准备晚饭。
example.pinyin: Jīnwǎn jiālǐ yǒu kèrén, wǒmen děi zhǔnbèi wǎnfàn.
example.english: We have guests at home tonight, so we need to prepare dinner.
example.fact: 客人 pairs 客 ("guest," built from a roof 宀 sheltering an arriving visitor 各) with the generic suffix 人 ("person") — the same 客 root gives 顾客 ("customer," a guest who pays) and 乘客 ("passenger," a guest riding along), all sharing the core image of someone welcomed in from outside.

components.note: 犬 (dog) — an old, now-opaque link behind 状's meaning 'form, shape, condition'
丬 (qiáng) gives a loose sound connection to 状's reading zhuàng
心 (heart/mind) — 态 relates to one's inner state, manner, or attitude
太 (tài) gives the sound — 态 is also pronounced tài, an exact match

example.hanzi: 他最近的身体状态不太好。
example.pinyin: Tā zuìjìn de shēntǐ zhuàngtài bú tài hǎo.
example.english: His physical condition hasn't been very good lately.
example.fact: 状态 is also the standard word for "state" in science class — 固态/液态/气态 (solid/liquid/gaseous state) all reuse the 态 root — and in sports and gaming slang, 状态好/状态不好 ("in good/bad form") has become a casual, everyday way to talk about how someone is performing on a given day.

components.note: 冂 depicts a boundary or border enclosing an area.
土 (earth/land) — the land enclosed within the border.
口 here depicts a well within that land — together giving 周 its early meaning of a bounded territory, and later 'circumference, week, the Zhou dynasty.'
囗 (an enclosure) — 围 relates to surrounding or encircling something
韦 (wéi) gives the sound — 围 is also pronounced wéi, an exact match

example.hanzi: 公园周围有很多商店。
example.pinyin: Gōngyuán zhōuwéi yǒu hěn duō shāngdiàn.
example.english: There are many shops around the park.
example.fact: 周围 combines two characters that both independently suggest enclosure — 周 (an old word for a bounded territory) and 围 ("to surround," built from the enclosure radical 囗) — reinforcing each other into a word that always describes the space encircling something, never a single point.

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 报 relates to taking action against someone.
卩 (a kneeling or bound person) — handling a wrongdoer and announcing the judgment gave 报 its meaning 'to report' or 'to announce.'
辶 (to walk) — 道 relates to a path or road one walks along.
首 (shǒu) is the historical phonetic element; its modern reading no longer resembles dào, a reminder that sound components can drift after thousands of years of pronunciation change.

example.hanzi: 这家电视台对这次事件做了详细的报道。
example.pinyin: Zhè jiā diànshìtái duì zhè cì shìjiàn zuò le xiángxì de bàodào.
example.english: This TV station did a detailed report on the incident.
example.fact: 报道 is the standard word for journalistic reporting, distinct from the similar-looking 报告 (bàogào, "a report" in the sense of a formal written document, like a school or business report) — despite differing by only one character, the two words are not interchangeable.

components.note: 彡 (shān) is the historical phonetic component of 参; sound change over time has left little resemblance to the modern reading cān

example.hanzi: 很多学生都参与了这次活动。
example.pinyin: Hěn duō xuésheng dōu cānyù le zhè cì huódòng.
example.english: Many students participated in this event.
example.fact: 参与 is a shade more formal than the everyday 参加 ("to take part in, attend") — 参与 often stresses being involved in a process or decision (参与决策, "to participate in decision-making"), while 参加 more simply names attending an event (参加聚会, "attend a party"), a nuance easy for learners to blur.

components.note: 辶 (walking/movement) — relates to 运's meaning 'to move, transport,' and by extension 'fortune,' the movement of one's life.
云 (yún) gives a sound hint — 运 is pronounced yùn, sharing the same base sound with a different tone.
力 (strength/force) — 动 relates to movement produced by exertion or force.

example.hanzi: 医生建议他每天运动半小时。
example.pinyin: Yīshēng jiànyì tā měitiān yùndòng bàn xiǎoshí.
example.english: The doctor recommended he exercise for half an hour every day.
example.fact: 运动 stretches across three registers at once — physics' "motion" (物体的运动), everyday "exercise" (as here), and history's capital-M "Movement" (五四运动, the May Fourth Movement) — all sharing the same underlying idea of something set in motion, whether a body, a muscle, or a whole society.

components.note: 彳 (to walk, step) — 彼 originally related to distance, extended to mean 'that, the other.'
皮 (pí) gives a sound close to bǐ.
匕 here relates to a person crouching or sitting — 此 originally pictured 'this place' where someone is.
止 (zhǐ) gives a hint of the sound — 此 is pronounced cǐ, sharing a similar final though the initial has shifted over time.

example.hanzi: 我们应该彼此信任。
example.pinyin: Wǒmen yīnggāi bǐcǐ xìnrèn.
example.english: We should trust each other.
example.fact: 彼此 fuses two demonstrative roots meaning "that" (彼) and "this" (此) into a single reciprocal pronoun — a compositional logic close to English's own "each other," which likewise builds a mutual idea by pairing two separate pointing words.

components.note: 艹 (grass) forms the top of the character.
木 (tree), sheltered beneath a covering, together depict plants flourishing, giving 荣 its meaning 'glory, prosperity.'
The upper part, related to 土, traditionally depicted one person's fate.
干 depicted a contrasting fate — the character set two outcomes side by side, with the fortunate one giving 幸 its meaning 'lucky, fortunate.'

example.hanzi: 能认识您,我感到很荣幸。
example.pinyin: Néng rènshi nín, wǒ gǎndào hěn róngxìng.
example.english: I feel very honored to meet you.
example.fact: 荣幸 sits at the formal, politeness-register end of Chinese — common in introductions and speeches (很荣幸认识您, "it's an honor to meet you") but rarely reached for over small, everyday favors, where English "honored" can sometimes sound sarcastic if overused casually; 荣幸 keeps a consistently sincere, formal tone instead.

components.note: 人 (people) over 云 (clouds/say) — a picture of people gathering and speaking together, related to 会's meanings 'to meet' and 'to know how to.'
讠 (speech) — relates to 议's meaning 'to discuss, deliberate; opinion.'
义 (yì) gives the sound — 议 is also pronounced yì, an exact match.

example.hanzi: 明天上午九点有一个重要的会议。
example.pinyin: Míngtiān shàngwǔ jiǔ diǎn yǒu yí gè zhòngyào de huìyì.
example.english: There's an important meeting tomorrow at nine in the morning.
example.fact: 会议 is the formal, official word for a scheduled meeting, the kind on a corporate calendar, while a casual get-together among friends is called 聚会 instead — both share the root 会 ("to meet, gather"), but their second halves signal a difference in register a bare dictionary entry doesn't always convey.

components.note: 至 (zhì, to arrive) — carries 到's core meaning, 'to reach, to arrive'
刂 (a form of 刀, dāo) gives a sound close to 到's pronunciation dào
辶 (walking/movement) — relates to 达's meaning 'to reach, arrive, achieve.'
大 (dà) gives the sound — 达 is pronounced dá, a close match sharing the same rhyme.

example.hanzi: 火车将于晚上八点到达北京。
example.pinyin: Huǒchē jiāng yú wǎnshàng bā diǎn dàodá Běijīng.
example.english: The train will arrive in Beijing at eight in the evening.
example.fact: 到达 is the formal, written-register match for the everyday spoken verb 到 — a train schedule or news report says 到达, but a friend texting you would more naturally just write 我到了 ("I've arrived") rather than the stiffer-sounding 我到达了.

components.note: 日 (sun) — 显 relates to something bright and clearly visible in the light
业 (yè) gives a loose sound connection to 显's reading xiǎn
A pictograph of an altar or offering table used in ancestor worship — presenting offerings extended to 示's meaning 'to show, display, indicate.'

example.hanzi: 数据显示,今年的销量比去年高。
example.pinyin: Shùjù xiǎnshì, jīnnián de xiāoliàng bǐ qùnián gāo.
example.english: The data shows that this year's sales are higher than last year's.
example.fact: 显示 is also the standard word for a computer or phone display — 显示器 is "monitor" and 显示屏 is "display screen" — extending its written-register sense of "to reveal, indicate" into the literal hardware that shows images on a screen.

components.note: 阝 (a mound or place) — 队 pictures people gathering together.
人 (person) — people gathering in one place gave 队 its meaning 'a team' or 'a line/queue.'
亻 (person) — 伍 counts out a group of people.
五 (five) — five 五 people 亻 standing together gave 伍 its meaning 'a squad of five, a group.'

example.hanzi: 一大早,门口就排起了长长的队伍。
example.pinyin: Yí dà zǎo, ménkǒu jiù pái qǐ le chángcháng de duìwu.
example.english: Early in the morning, a long line had already formed at the entrance.
example.fact: 队伍 originally described soldiers marching in formation, but modern usage has broadened it into the everyday word for any line of people waiting — 排队伍, alongside the more common 排队 ("to queue"), still draws on the same military image of people falling into an orderly row.

components.note: 立 depicts a person standing with arms and legs spread, on a horizontal line representing the ground — a simple picture of standing upright.
刂 (a knife) — 刻 relates to carving with a blade
亥 (hài) is the historical phonetic element; it no longer closely matches 刻's modern reading kè

example.hanzi: 听到消息后,他立刻打电话给妈妈。
example.pinyin: Tīngdào xiāoxi hòu, tā lìkè dǎ diànhuà gěi māma.
example.english: After hearing the news, he immediately called his mom.
example.fact: 立刻 sits among a cluster of near-synonymous "immediately" adverbs — 马上, 立刻, and 立即 — that are largely interchangeable in casual speech, with 立即 leaning slightly more formal and written, a register distinction dictionaries rarely spell out for near-synonyms.

components.note: 纟 (thread) — 绝 originally meant to sever a thread completely, extended to mean 'to cut off, absolute'
色 (sè) gives a loose sound connection to 绝's reading jué
The oracle-bone form has been interpreted as a bird flying up toward the sky; the meaning later shifted entirely to represent negation, 'not.'

example.hanzi: 我绝不会放弃我的梦想。
example.pinyin: Wǒ jué bú huì fàngqì wǒ de mèngxiǎng.
example.english: I will never give up on my dream.
example.fact: 绝 already means "to cut off completely" on its own (绝望 "to give up hope," 绝交 "to break off a friendship") — prefixed onto 不, it turns a plain negative into an emphatic one, working like English "absolutely not" rather than a soft "not really."

components.note: 無-shaped top pictures a dancer holding decorated sleeves or fans.
舛 below pictures a pair of feet, together giving 舞 its meaning 'to dance.'

example.hanzi: 她第一次站在舞台上唱歌,非常紧张。
example.pinyin: Tā dì-yī cì zhàn zài wǔtái shàng chàng gē, fēicháng jǐnzhāng.
example.english: The first time she stood on stage to sing, she was extremely nervous.
example.fact: 舞台 literally means "dance platform" (舞 "to dance" + 台 "platform, stage") — even though modern stages host far more than dance, from theater to political speeches (政治舞台, "the political stage/arena"), the word still carries its original image of a raised performance space.

components.note: 女 (woman) — 奶 relates to a woman nursing, and to milk.
乃 (nǎi) is an exact match for the sound of 奶.
女 (woman) — 奶 relates to a woman nursing, and to milk.
乃 (nǎi) is an exact match for the sound of 奶.

example.hanzi: 我奶奶今年八十岁了,身体还很健康。
example.pinyin: Wǒ nǎinai jīnnián bāshí suì le, shēntǐ hái hěn jiànkāng.
example.english: My grandma is eighty this year and still in good health.
example.fact: Chinese kinship terms are far more specific than English's single "grandma" — 奶奶 names your father's mother specifically, while your mother's mother is a different word, 外婆 (or 姥姥 in northern usage) — the two sides of the family tree are never collapsed into one shared term the way English does.

components.note: 又 (a hand) — reaching to take hold of something.
耳 (ear) — from an ancient battlefield practice of taking a fallen enemy's ear as proof of a kill, the origin of 取's meaning 'to take, obtain.'
氵 (water) — relates to 消's meaning 'to disappear, dissolve,' like something dissolving in water.
肖 (xiào) gives a sound hint — 消 is pronounced xiāo, sharing the same base sound with a different tone.

example.hanzi: 因为天气不好,航班被取消了。
example.pinyin: Yīnwèi tiānqì bù hǎo, hángbān bèi qǔxiāo le.
example.english: The flight was canceled because of bad weather.
example.fact: 取消 reads almost literally as "take away until it vanishes" — 取 ("to take, obtain," from an old image of taking an ear as spoils) plus 消 ("to dissolve, vanish") — a small window into how many Chinese two-character verbs are built by stacking a concrete action onto its intended result.

components.note: 亠 — read as the head of an animal standing upright in this pictograph; the character was later reused for the unrelated meaning 'to leave, be apart from, distance.'
女 (woman) — 婚 relates to marriage, historically centered on the wife.
昏 (hūn) gives the sound — an exact match with 婚.

example.hanzi: 他们结婚三年后决定离婚。
example.pinyin: Tāmen jiéhūn sān nián hòu juédìng líhūn.
example.english: They decided to divorce three years after getting married.
example.fact: 离婚 and 结婚 ("to marry") form a natural opposite pair through their first characters alone — 离 ("to leave, separate") versus 结 ("to tie, bind") — a vivid shared image of marriage as a knot and divorce as its undoing.

components.note: ⺮ (bamboo) — 等 pictures bamboo strips, once used as writing tablets, being sorted.
寺 (originally a government office, later 'temple') — sorting and arranging bamboo documents at an official court gave 等 its meanings 'to wait,' 'rank,' and 'etc.'
彳 (a road/step) — someone arriving on the road
寺 (a court/hall) — the destination where the visitor is welcomed

example.hanzi: 我们已经等待这个结果很久了。
example.pinyin: Wǒmen yǐjīng děngdài zhège jiéguǒ hěn jiǔ le.
example.english: We have been waiting for this result for a long time.
example.fact: 等待 is the formal, written-register partner of the everyday verb 等 — you'd say 等我一下 ("wait for me a sec") in casual speech, but a news report or literary text would more likely reach for 等待, as in 等待救援 ("waiting for rescue").

components.note: 冖 (a roof/house) — the home being welcomed into.
友 (a friend) — brought close into one's home; the traditional form 愛 also includes 心 ('heart') in the middle — the source of 爱's meaning 'to love.'
忄 (heart) — 情 relates to feelings and emotions.
青 (qīng) gives the sound — 情 is pronounced qíng, a close match differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 这部小说讲的是一段悲伤的爱情故事。
example.pinyin: Zhè bù xiǎoshuō jiǎng de shì yí duàn bēishāng de àiqíng gùshi.
example.english: This novel tells a sad love story.
example.fact: Chinese splits "love" by object in a way English doesn't: 爱情 is reserved specifically for romantic love between partners, while love for family, friends, or country uses plain 爱 or compounds like 亲情 (family love) and 友情 (friendship) — there's no single all-purpose word covering every kind of love the way English "love" does.

components.note: 力 depicts the blade of a plow — since plowing fields took great physical effort, the shape came to represent strength or power.

example.hanzi: 不管结果如何,我都会尽力。
example.pinyin: Bùguǎn jiéguǒ rúhé, wǒ dōu huì jìnlì.
example.english: No matter what the result is, I'll do my best.
example.fact: 尽力 literally means "to exhaust one's strength" (尽 "to use up completely" + 力 "strength, power") — the same 尽 root shows up in 尽量 ("as much as possible") and 尽情 ("to one's heart's content"), all sharing the sense of pushing something all the way to its limit.

components.note: 八 (to divide/split apart) — represents something already split into parts.
刀 (knife) — a knife cutting already-divided pieces further, giving 分 its meaning 'to divide, to separate.'

example.hanzi: 这个消息让大家十分惊讶。
example.pinyin: Zhège xiāoxi ràng dàjiā shífēn jīngyà.
example.english: This news made everyone extremely surprised.
example.fact: 十分 literally means "ten parts" — the same logic as saying something is "a hundred percent" true in English — turning a picture of a whole divided into ten complete parts into an intensifier meaning "extremely, thoroughly."

components.note: 酋 pictures a jar of wine.
寸 (hand) below offers it up respectfully, giving 尊 its meaning 'to respect, to honor.'
千 (thousand) — 重 pictures a heavy burden carried a great distance.
里 (a unit of distance, like a mile) — carrying something a thousand 里 emphasizes how heavy and significant a burden it is, giving 重 its meaning 'heavy' or 'important.'

example.hanzi: 我们应该尊重每一个人的意见。
example.pinyin: Wǒmen yīnggāi zūnzhòng měi yí gè rén de yìjiàn.
example.english: We should respect everyone's opinions.
example.fact: 尊 alone pictures a wine jar 酋 lifted up by a hand 寸 — a gesture of offering made to an honored guest or ancestor — while 重 contributes the idea of "weight, importance"; together 尊重 treats respect almost literally as "holding someone up as important."

components.note: 攵 (a hand with a stick) — 教 relates to instructing or disciplining, the traditional action of teaching.
孝 (xiào) gives a hint of the sound — 教 is pronounced jiào, a connection that has shifted somewhat.
扌 (hand) — 授 means to give or hand something over.
受 (shòu) gives the sound — an exact match with 授.

example.hanzi: 张教授在国际会议上发表了演讲。
example.pinyin: Zhāng jiàoshòu zài guójì huìyì shàng fābiǎo le yǎnjiǎng.
example.english: Professor Zhang gave a speech at the international conference.
example.fact: 教授 is a genuine tone-based homograph: read jiàoshòu (as corrected here, 4th-tone 教) it's the everyday noun "professor" — overwhelmingly the common sense at this frequency, from news mentions of faculty to forms of address like 张教授 — while read jiāoshòu (1st-tone 教) it becomes a formal verb meaning "to instruct in a subject." The same split separates the everyday teaching verb 教 (jiāo, as in 教书) from the noun-forming reading 教 (jiào, as in 教育 "education").

components.note: 干 (originally a person) shown carrying a heavy load of grain on their back — since harvests came once a year, the character came to mean 'year.'

example.hanzi: 去年夏天,我们去了云南旅行。
example.pinyin: Qùnián xiàtiān, wǒmen qù le Yúnnán lǜxíng.
example.english: Last summer, we traveled to Yunnan.
example.fact: 去年 uses 去 in its older sense of "past, gone by" rather than its everyday meaning "to go" — the same "past" sense survives in 去世 ("to pass away," lit. "to depart the world") — so 去年 literally reads as "the year gone by," a mirror image of 明年 ("next year") and 今年 ("this year").

components.note: 走 (to walk/run) — 超 relates to overtaking or surpassing someone while moving
召 (zhào) gives a sound distantly related to 超's reading chāo, having drifted apart over time
辶 (to walk/move) — shows 过's core meaning of 'passing through' or 'crossing'
咼 (guō) gives a sound close to 过's reading guò; the simplified form 过 now uses 寸 in place of 咼, but the phonetic connection traces back to the traditional character 過

example.hanzi: 参加比赛的人数超过了两百人。
example.pinyin: Cānjiā bǐsài de rénshù chāoguò le liǎng bǎi rén.
example.english: The number of people participating in the competition exceeded two hundred.
example.fact: 超过 combines 超 ("to overtake while running," built from 走 "to walk/run") with 过 ("to pass by, cross over") — both halves independently picture motion going beyond a point, reinforcing each other into a word that always implies comparison against some threshold or rival.

components.note: 廾 (two hands) — depicts hands at work.
一 represents the latch or bar of a door; hands lifting it away gave 开 its meaning 'to open, to start.'
A simplified form of 車, a pictograph of a two-wheeled cart seen from above — the wheels, axle, and frame are visible in the original shape — the source of 车's meaning 'cart, vehicle.'

example.hanzi: 他每天开车去上班。
example.pinyin: Tā měitiān kāichē qù shàngbān.
example.english: He drives to work every day.
example.fact: 开车 literally means "to open/operate a car" — the same verb 开 that "opens" a door or a book also "operates" machines and vehicles in Chinese (开灯 "turn on the light," 开会 "hold a meeting"), a much broader use of "open" than English's narrower literal sense.

meanings: the arches, loops and whorls on the fingers

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 指 relates to using the hand, specifically the fingers.
旨 (an aim, purpose) — combined with 扌 (hand), 指 came to mean 'finger' and 'to point,' aiming the hand at something.
Thread/silk — patterns were originally woven into cloth.
Gives the sound wén, matching the character's reading.

example.hanzi: 手机可以用指纹解锁。
example.pinyin: Shǒujī kěyǐ yòng zhǐwén jiěsuǒ.
example.english: You can unlock the phone using your fingerprint.
example.fact: 指纹 combines 指 ("finger") with 纹 ("pattern, grain" — the same root behind 花纹 "decorative pattern" and 纹路 "grain lines"), treating a fingerprint as just one more example of a natural surface pattern, the same way wood grain or a leaf's veins would be described.

components.note: 广 (a building/shelter) — the setting of the celebration.
大 (great, big) — a grand event held inside, together giving 庆 its meaning 'to celebrate.'
礻 (altar, spirit) on the left sets a religious scene.
兄 (a person, shown here kneeling or speaking) on the right shows someone praying, giving 祝 its meaning 'to wish, to pray for blessings.'

example.hanzi: 我们打算庆祝他的生日。
example.pinyin: Wǒmen dǎsuàn qìngzhù tā de shēngrì.
example.english: We plan to celebrate his birthday.
example.fact: 庆祝 reinforces two overlapping ideas — 庆 ("to celebrate," pictured as a grand event 大 held under a roof 广) and 祝 ("to wish, pray for blessings," with the altar radical 礻) — pairing a worldly celebration with a spoken blessing, the same double-barreled word-building strategy seen in 喜欢 and 应该 in the character deck's own word list.

components.note: 亻 (person) — the one settling somewhere.
主 (host, master) — the idea of a person settled in a place as if hosting it, giving 住 its meaning 'to live, reside, stay.'
手 is a simple picture of an open hand with the fingers spread out.

example.hanzi: 住手!你会伤到他的。
example.pinyin: Zhùshǒu! Nǐ huì shāng dào tā de.
example.english: Stop! You'll hurt him.
example.fact: 住手 literally means "to halt the hand" (住 "to stop, stay" + 手 "hand") — used as a sharp command, it belongs to a small family of "stop + body part" imperatives that includes 住口 ("shut your mouth," lit. "stop the mouth"), each naming the specific body part responsible for the unwanted action.

components.note: 亻 (person) — 偶 originally described a wooden figure or idol shaped like a person, later extending to 'a pair' and 'by chance.'
禺 (yú) gives a sound distantly related to 偶's reading ǒu, having drifted apart over time.
亻 (person) — relates to 像's meaning 'to resemble, be like; image, portrait,' comparing one person or thing to another.
象 (xiàng) gives the sound — 像 is also pronounced xiàng, an exact match.

example.hanzi: 很多年轻人把这位歌手当作自己的偶像。
example.pinyin: Hěn duō niánqīng rén bǎ zhè wèi gēshǒu dàngzuò zìjǐ de ǒuxiàng.
example.english: Many young people regard this singer as their idol.
example.fact: 偶像 originally referred literally to a carved wooden or clay figure worshipped as a god — 偶 (from the person radical 亻) meant "a figure, statue" before it took on its other senses "by chance" and "a couple" — and the compound carried that image of a worshipped effigy forward into its modern, secular sense of a celebrity idolized by fans.

components.note: 凡 (common/ordinary) — suggests something shared or held in common.
口 (mouth) — sharing a common mouth/voice with others gave 同 its meaning of 'same, together.'
士 (a scholar/gentleman) — represents a person of learning and ambition.
心 (heart/mind) — the mind and aspirations of a scholar gave 志 its meaning 'purpose, will, ambition.'

example.hanzi: 各位同志,请注意会议时间的变化。
example.pinyin: Gèwèi tóngzhì, qǐng zhùyì huìyì shíjiān de biànhuà.
example.english: Comrades, please note the change in meeting time.
example.fact: 同志 literally means "same aspiration" (同 "same" + 志 "ambition, will") and was the standard, egalitarian form of address in Mao-era China, much as "comrade" was used in other socialist movements; since around the late 1980s it has also become common slang for "homosexual" in Chinese-speaking communities, an entirely separate modern reappropriation of the same old political word.

components.note: 衤 (clothes) — 裤 names a piece of clothing, trousers.
库 (kù) gives the sound — an exact match with 裤.
A simple drawing of a swaddled baby — arms reaching out, legs bundled together in a wrap.

example.hanzi: 这条裤子有点儿长,得改一改。
example.pinyin: Zhè tiáo kùzi yǒudiǎnr cháng, děi gǎi yi gǎi.
example.english: These pants are a bit long; they need to be altered.
example.fact: 裤子 takes the clothing radical 衤 (a compressed form of 衣, "clothing," also seen in 衬衫 "shirt" and 裙子 "skirt") paired with the phonetic 库 (kù, "storehouse") purely for its sound — a reminder that the radical, not the phonetic half, is usually the more reliable guide to a character's meaning.

components.note: 冖 here is a distorted form of 力 (strength) — a simplified way of showing soldiers grouped together.
车 (cart/vehicle) — 军 originally pictured soldiers riding out to battle in war chariots.
阝 (a mound or place) — 队 pictures people gathering together.
人 (person) — people gathering in one place gave 队 its meaning 'a team' or 'a line/queue.'

example.hanzi: 这个国家的军队负责保卫边境。
example.pinyin: Zhège guójiā de jūnduì fùzé bǎowèi biānjìng.
example.english: This country's military is responsible for defending the border.
example.fact: 军队 combines 军 (an old pictograph of soldiers riding out in war chariots 车) with 队 ("a team, a file of people," from an image of people 人 gathered together) — forming the general word for any organized armed force, from a national army down to a smaller unit.
